questions.question: A machine has a 32-bit architecture, with 1-word long instructions. It has 64 registers, each of  which is 32 bits long. It needs to support 45 instructions, which have an immediate operand in addition to two register operands. Assuming that the immediate operand is an unsigned integer, the maximum value of the immediate operand is ____________.

Checking each statement:
- 45 instructions [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 6-bit opcode
- 2 registers of 64 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 6 + 6 = 12 bits
- Immediate = 32 [latex]-[/latex] 6 [latex]-[/latex] 12 = 14 bits [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] max unsigned value [latex]2^{14}-1=16383[/latex]

Answer: 16383

questions.question:
A keyboard connected to a computer is used at a rate of 1 keystroke per second. The computer system polls the keyboard every 10 ms (milli seconds) to check for a keystroke and consumes 100 [latex] \mu s[/latex] (micro seconds) for each poll. If it is determined after polling that a key has been pressed, the system consumes an additional 200 [latex] \mu s[/latex] to process the keystroke. Let [latex] T_1[/latex] denote the fraction of a second spent in polling and processing a keystroke.
In an alternative implementation, the system uses interrupts instead of polling. An interrupt is raised for every keystroke. It takes a total of 1 ms for servicing an interrupt and processing a keystroke. Let [latex] T_2[/latex] denote the fraction of a second spent in servicing the interrupt and processing a keystroke. The ratio [latex] \frac{T_1}{T_2}[/latex] is ______ . (Rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation:
Polling: 100 polls per second (every 10 ms) [latex]\times[/latex] 100 [latex]\mu[/latex]s = 10 ms, plus 200 [latex]\mu[/latex]s for the one keystroke [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]T_1=10.2[/latex] ms per second.

Interrupts: one keystroke per second [latex]\times[/latex] 1 ms [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]T_2=1[/latex] ms per second.

[latex]\frac{T_1}{T_2}=\frac{10.2}{1}=10.2[/latex]

Answer: 10.2

questions.question:
Consider a 6-stage instruction pipeline, where all stages are perfectly balanced. Assume that
there is no cycle-time overhead of pipelining. When an application is executing on this 6-stage pipeline, the speedup achieved with respect to non-pipelined execution if 25% of the instructions incur 2 pipeline stall cycles is _________.
questions.explanation:
Pipelined CPI = 1 + 0.25 [latex]\times[/latex] 2 = 1.5. A balanced 6-stage pipeline ideally gives speedup 6.

Speedup = 6 / 1.5 = 4

Answer: 4

questions.question:
Consider a system with a processor and a [latex]4[/latex] KB direct mapped cache with block size of [latex]16[/latex] bytes. The system has a [latex]16[/latex] MB physical memory. Four words [latex]{P}, {Q}, {R}[/latex], and S are accessed by the processor in the same order [latex]10[/latex] times. That is, there are a total of [latex]40[/latex] memory references in the sequence [latex]{P}, {Q}, {R}, {S}, {P}, {Q}, {R}, {S}, \ldots[/latex]

Assume that the cache memory is initially empty. The physical addresses of the words are given below ([latex]1[/latex] word [latex]=1[/latex] byte).

[latex]\text{P: 0x845B32, Q: 0x845B26, R: 0x845B36, S: 0x846B32}[/latex]

Which of the following statements is/are true?
Note: [latex]1 {~K}=2^{10}[/latex] and [latex]1 {M}=2^{20}[/latex]

options.A: Every access to [latex]\text{P}[/latex] results in a cache miss
options.B: Every access to [latex]\text{R}[/latex] results in a cache hit
options.C: Every access to [latex]\text{Q}[/latex] results in a cache miss
options.D: Except the first access to [latex]\text{S}[/latex], all subsequent accesses to [latex]\text{S}[/latex] result in cache hits

questions.explanation:
Cache: [latex]4[/latex] KB, block size [latex]16[/latex] bytes [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] offset [latex]=4[/latex] bits, number of lines [latex]=4096/16=256=2^8\Rightarrow[/latex] index [latex]=8[/latex] bits; physical memory [latex]16[/latex] MB [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] address width [latex]=24[/latex] bits, so tag [latex]=24-8-4=12[/latex] bits.

Computing (block-address, index, tag) for each word shows that [latex]P=0\text{x}845B32[/latex] and [latex]R=0\text{x}845B36[/latex] fall in the same [latex]16[/latex]-byte block (both addresses lie within [latex]0\text{x}845B30[/latex]-[latex]0\text{x}845B3F[/latex]), while [latex]Q=0\text{x}845B26[/latex] maps to a different cache line (a different index) than [latex]P/R[/latex], and [latex]S=0\text{x}846B32[/latex] maps to the same index as [latex]P/R[/latex] but with a different tag (so [latex]S[/latex] conflicts with [latex]P/R[/latex]'s cache line).

Simulating the repeating access sequence [latex]P,Q,R,S,P,Q,R,S,\ldots[/latex]: each [latex]S[/latex] access evicts the [latex]P/R[/latex] block (same index, different tag), so the very next [latex]P[/latex] access is always a fresh miss (reloading [latex]P[/latex]'s block, which also brings in [latex]R[/latex] since they share a block); the following [latex]R[/latex] access is then always a hit (block was just loaded by [latex]P[/latex]); and the following [latex]S[/latex] access is always a miss again (conflicts with the just-refreshed [latex]P/R[/latex] tag). Meanwhile [latex]Q[/latex]'s index never conflicts with anything else, so only its very first access misses; all later [latex]Q[/latex] accesses are hits (not "every access misses").

Answer: Every access to P is a miss, and every access to R is a hit.

questions.question:
For a direct-mapped cache, 4 bits are used for the tag field and 12 bits are used to index into a cache block. The size of each cache block is one byte. Assume that there is no other information stored for each cache block.
Which ONE of the following is the CORRECT option for the sizes of the main memory and the cache memory in this system (byte addressable), respectively?
questions.explanation:
Block size [latex]=1[/latex] byte [latex]=2^0[/latex], so the offset field needs [latex]0[/latex] bits. With [latex]12[/latex]-bit index and [latex]4[/latex]-bit tag, the total address width [latex]=4+12+0=16[/latex] bits.

Main memory size [latex]=2^{16}=65536[/latex] bytes [latex]=64[/latex] KB.

Cache size [latex]=[/latex] (number of lines) [latex]\times[/latex] (block size) [latex]=2^{12}\times1=4096[/latex] bytes [latex]=4[/latex] KB.

Answer: 64 KB and 4 KB

questions.question:
A five-stage pipeline has stage delays of 150, 120, 150, 160 and 140 nanoseconds. The registers that are used between the pipeline stages have a delay of 5 nanoseconds each.
The total time to execute 100 independent instructions on this pipeline, assuming there are no pipeline stalls, is _______ nanoseconds.
questions.explanation:
Clock cycle = slowest stage + register delay = 160 + 5 = 165 ns.
Cycles for 100 instructions on 5 stages = 5 + 100 [latex]-[/latex] 1 = 104.

Time = 104 [latex]\times[/latex] 165 = 17160 ns

Answer: 17160

questions.question:
Consider the following instruction sequence where registers [latex]R_1,R_2 \text{ and }R_3[/latex] are general purpose and [latex]MEMORY[X][/latex] denotes the content at the memory location [latex]X[/latex].

[latex]\begin{array}{llc} \textbf{Instruction} & \textbf{Semantics} & \textbf{Instruction Size} \text{ (bytes)} \\ \hline \text{MOV } R1, (5000) & R1 \leftarrow \text{MEMORY}[5000] & 4 \\ \hline \text{MOV } R2, (R3) & R2 \leftarrow \text{MEMORY}[R3] & 4 \\ \hline \text{ADD} R2, R1 & R2 \leftarrow R1 + R2 & 2 \\ \hline \text{MOV } (R3), R2 & \text{MEMORY}[R3] \leftarrow R2 & 4 \\ \hline \text{INC } R3 & R3 \leftarrow R3+1 & 2 \\ \hline \text{DEC } R1 & R1 \leftarrow R1-1 & 2 \\ \hline \text{BNZ } 1004 & \text{Branch if not zero to the} & 2 \\ & \text{given absolute address} \\ \hline \text{HALT} & \text{Stop} & 1 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]

Assume that the content of the memory location 5000 is 10, and the content of the register [latex]R_3[/latex] is 3000. The content of each of the memory locations from 3000 to 3020 is 50. The instruction sequence starts from the memory location 1000. All the numbers are in decimal format. Assume that the memory is byte addressable.
After the execution of the program, the content of memory location 3010 is ____________
questions.explanation:
R1 = MEMORY[5000] = 10, so the loop (BNZ back to 1004) runs 10 times. Each pass adds R1 to MEMORY[R3] and moves R3 one byte ahead.

R3 goes 3000, 3001, [latex]\ldots[/latex], 3009. Location 3010 is never written, so it keeps its value 50.

Answer: 50

questions.question:
A computer has a 256 KByte, 4-way set associative, write back data cache with block size of 32 Bytes. The processor sends 32 bit addresses to the cache controller. Each cache tag directory entry contains, in addition to address tag, 2 valid bits, 1 modified bit and 1 replacement bit.

The number of bits in the tag field of an address is
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Blocks = 256 KB / 32 B = 8192, sets = 8192 / 4 = 2048 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] index = 11 bits
- Offset = 5 bits

Tag = 32 [latex]-[/latex] 11 [latex]-[/latex] 5 = 16 bits

Answer: 16

questions.question:
Consider a 2-way set associative cache with 256 blocks and uses LRU replacement, Initially the cache is empty. Conflict misses are those misses which occur due the contention of multiple blocks for the same cache set. Compulsory misses occur due to first time access to the block. The following sequence of accesses to memory blocks.

(0,128,256,128,0,128,256,128,1,129,257,129,1,129,257,129)

is repeated 10 times. The number of conflict misses experienced by the cache is ___________.
questions.explanation:
128 sets (2-way). Blocks 0, 128, 256 map to set 0; 1, 129, 257 map to set 1. Set 0 sees 0, 128, 256, 128, 0, 128, 256, 128 each round:
- Round 1: 0, 128, 256 are compulsory misses; then 0 and 256 miss again (conflict) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 conflict misses.
- Each later round: 0 and 256 keep evicting each other (128 stays) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4 conflict misses.

Set 0: 2 + 9 [latex]\times[/latex] 4 = 38. Set 1 behaves the same: 38. Total = 76

Answer: 76

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.question:
A computer has a 256 KByte, 4-way set associative, write back data cache with block size of 32 Bytes. The processor sends 32 bit addresses to the cache controller. Each cache tag directory entry contains, in addition to address tag, 2 valid bits, 1 modified bit and 1 replacement bit.

The size of the cache tag directory is
questions.explanation:
Each entry = 16 (tag) + 2 (valid) + 1 (modified) + 1 (replacement) = 20 bits. There are 8192 entries (one per block).

8192 [latex]\times[/latex] 20 = 163840 bits = 160 Kbits

Answer: 160 Kbits

questions.question:
A processor has 64 general-purpose registers and 50 distinct instruction types. An instruction is encoded in 32-bits. What is the maximum number of bits that can be used to store the immediate operand for the given instruction?

ADD R1, #25 // R1 = R1 + 25
questions.explanation:
With [latex]64=2^6[/latex] registers, each register-number field needs [latex]6[/latex] bits. With [latex]50[/latex] distinct instruction types, the opcode field needs [latex]\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=6[/latex] bits (since [latex]2^5=32<50\le64=2^6[/latex]).

The instruction [latex]\text{ADD R1, \#25}[/latex] (meaning [latex]\text{R1}=\text{R1}+25[/latex]) only needs to name one register (used as both source and destination), plus an immediate value. So the [latex]32[/latex]-bit instruction splits as: opcode ([latex]6[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] one register field ([latex]6[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] immediate field (the rest).

Immediate field width [latex]=32-6-6=20[/latex] bits.

Answer: 20

Click here for detail solution

questions.question:
If the associativity of a processor cache is doubled while keeping the capacity and block size
unchanged, which one of the following is guaranteed to be NOT affected?

options.D: Width of processor to main memory data bus

questions.explanation:
Doubling associativity halves the number of sets: the index loses 1 bit, the tag gains 1 bit, and the way multiplexer gets twice the inputs.

The processor-to-memory data bus width does not depend on cache organisation.

Answer: Width of processor to main memory data bus

questions.question:
Consider a 512 GB hard disk with 32 storage surfaces. There are 4096 sectors per
track and each sector holds 1024 bytes of data. The number of cylinders in the hard
disk is ____
questions.explanation:
Capacity = cylinders [latex]\times[/latex] surfaces [latex]\times[/latex] sectors per track [latex]\times[/latex] bytes per sector.

[latex]512\text{ GB}=2^{39}[/latex], 32 surfaces [latex]=2^5[/latex], 4096 sectors [latex]=2^{12}[/latex], 1024 bytes [latex]=2^{10}[/latex].

Cylinders [latex]=\dfrac{2^{39}}{2^5\times2^{12}\times2^{10}}=2^{12}=4096[/latex]

Answer: 4096
